claim: Dendritic coincidence detection is fundamental to neuronal processing yet remains largely unexplored in awake animals.
source: Dendritic coincidence detection is fundamental to neuronal processing yet remains largely unexplored in awake animals.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by the context of existing literature and the novelty of the current study.

claim: The underlying dendritic voltage–calcium relationship has not been directly addressed in awake animals.
source: Specifically, the underlying dendritic voltage–calcium relationship has not been directly addressed.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Simultaneous voltage and calcium two-photon imaging of Purkinje neuron spiny dendrites was used to study coincident synaptic inputs in awake mice.
source: Here, using simultaneous voltage and calcium two-photon imaging of Purkinje neuron spiny dendrites, we show how coincident synaptic inputs and resulting dendritic spikes modulate dendritic calcium signaling during sensory stimulation in awake mice.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Sensory stimulation increased the rate of postsynaptic potentials and dendritic calcium spikes evoked by climbing fiber and parallel fiber synaptic input.
source: Sensory stimulation increased the rate of postsynaptic potentials and dendritic calcium spikes evoked by climbing fiber and parallel fiber synaptic input.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Climbing fiber and parallel fiber inputs are integrated in a time-dependent and nonlinear fashion to enhance the sensory-evoked dendritic calcium signal.
source: These inputs are integrated in a time-dependent and nonlinear fashion to enhance the sensory-evoked dendritic calcium signal.
evidence: This is a primary finding describing the nature of synaptic integration observed in the study.

claim: Intrinsic supralinear dendritic mechanisms, including voltage-gated calcium channels and metabotropic glutamate receptors, are recruited cooperatively to expand the dynamic range of sensory-evoked dendritic calcium signals.
source: Intrinsic supralinear dendritic mechanisms, including voltage-gated calcium channels and metabotropic glutamate receptors, are recruited cooperatively to expand the dynamic range of sensory-evoked dendritic calcium signals.
evidence: This is a primary finding identifying specific molecular mechanisms involved in dendritic integration.

claim: Most studies on dendritic integration have been performed in vitro, in the absence of physiological inputs.
source: So far, most studies on dendritic integration have been performed in vitro, in the absence of physiological inputs (Larkum et al., 2009; Markram et al., 1997; Stuart and Häusser, 2001; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Equivalent in vivo studies on dendritic integration are essential for exploring how dendritic integration works in living animals.
source: Equivalent in vivo studies, though technically challenging, are essential for exploring how dendritic integration works in living animals (Chen et al., 2013; Jia et al., 2010; Murayama et al., 2009; Palmer et al., 2014; Sheffield and Dombeck, 2015; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vivo studies and represents a consensus in the field.

claim: In vivo patch clamp recordings targeting the soma or smooth dendrites cannot directly measure signals in the most distal dendritic regions that receive the majority of synaptic input.
source: Notably, in vivo patch clamp recordings targeting the soma or smooth dendrites cannot directly measure signals in the most distal dendritic regions that receive the majority of synaptic input, called the 'spiny' dendrites.
evidence: This describes a technical limitation of conventional recording methods.

claim: In vivo calcium imaging from spiny dendrites can partially circumvent the limitation of patch clamp recordings.
source: In vivo calcium imaging from spiny dendrites can partially circumvent this issue (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Calcium imaging omits the depolarizing and hyperpolarizing voltage signals evoked by synaptic input that do not trigger postsynaptic calcium signals.
source: However, this approach measures dendritic calcium events only and omits the depolarizing and hyperpolarizing voltage signals evoked by synaptic input that do not trigger postsynaptic calcium signals.
evidence: This describes a limitation of calcium imaging approaches.

claim: Synaptic potentials are expected to generate continuous but highly inhomogeneous spatiotemporal dendritic activity in awake animals.
source: These synaptic potentials are expected to generate continuous but highly inhomogeneous spatiotemporal dendritic activity in awake animals.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the nature of synaptic inputs.

claim: A glimpse of continuous spatiotemporal dendritic activity was shown in the cerebellar Purkinje neuron.
source: A glimpse of this was shown in the cerebellar Purkinje neuron (PN) (Roome and Kuhn, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Neurons distinguish important signals from ongoing synaptic activity by amplifying dendritic voltage signals as part of ongoing synaptic integration.
source: By detecting coincident synaptic input, it is thought that neurons distinguish important signals from ongoing synaptic activity by amplifying dendritic voltage signals as part of ongoing synaptic integration (Stuart and Häusser, 2001) and by modifying synaptic strength through synaptic plasticity (Brown et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Neurons modify synaptic strength through synaptic plasticity as part of coincidence detection.
source: By detecting coincident synaptic input, it is thought that neurons distinguish important signals from ongoing synaptic activity by amplifying dendritic voltage signals as part of ongoing synaptic integration (Stuart and Häusser, 2001) and by modifying synaptic strength through synaptic plasticity (Brown et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on synaptic plasticity.

claim: Purkinje neuron dendrites are ideally suited to perform coincidence detection.
source: PN dendrites are ideally suited to perform coincidence detection.
evidence: This is based on the known anatomy and physiology of Purkinje neurons.

claim: Purkinje neurons receive excitatory synaptic input from two distinct pathways: a single climbing fiber and numerous parallel fibers.
source: They receive excitatory synaptic input from two distinct pathways: a single climbing fiber (CF) and numerous parallel fibers (PFs).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about Purkinje neurons.

claim: Climbing fibers project from the inferior olive and evoke reliable dendritic calcium spikes.
source: CFs project from the inferior olive and evoke reliable dendritic calcium spikes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about climbing fiber inputs to Purkinje neurons.

claim: Parallel fibers relay mossy fiber activity originating from multiple brainstem nuclei.
source: PFs relay mossy fiber (MF) activity originating from multiple brainstem nuclei, and together with synaptic input from inhibitory molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) elicit postsynaptic potentials in the PN dendrites (Kitamura and Häusser, 2011; Konnerth et al., 1990; Roome and Kuhn, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on cerebellar circuitry.

claim: Parallel fibers together with synaptic input from inhibitory molecular layer interneurons elicit postsynaptic potentials in Purkinje neuron dendrites.
source: PFs relay mossy fiber (MF) activity originating from multiple brainstem nuclei, and together with synaptic input from inhibitory molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) elicit postsynaptic potentials in the PN dendrites (Kitamura and Häusser, 2011; Konnerth et al., 1990; Roome and Kuhn, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In cerebellar slices, paired stimulation of parallel fiber and climbing fiber input evoke supralinear dendritic calcium signals in Purkinje neurons.
source: In cerebellar slices, paired stimulation of PF and CF input evoke 'supralinear' dendritic calcium signals in PNs, whereby the signal amplitude is larger than the sum of calcium signals triggered by PF and CF input alone.
evidence: This describes findings from previous in vitro studies.

claim: Supralinear calcium signals at parallel fiber-Purkinje neuron synapses lead to long-term depression.
source: At PF–PN synapses these supralinear calcium signals lead to a form of synaptic plasticity, known as long-term depression (LTD) (Miyata et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on synaptic plasticity.

claim: Coincidence detection in Purkinje neuron spines and dendrites is well studied in cerebellar slices.
source: This particular coincidence detection process is well studied in PN spines and dendrites in cerebellar slices, and supports early theoretical predictions for motor learning in the cerebellum whereby the CF input is thought to serve as an instructive 'teaching' signal that modifies PF synaptic input through induction of LTD (Marr, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and theoretical predictions.

claim: The climbing fiber input is thought to serve as an instructive 'teaching' signal that modifies parallel fiber synaptic input through induction of long-term depression.
source: This particular coincidence detection process is well studied in PN spines and dendrites in cerebellar slices, and supports early theoretical predictions for motor learning in the cerebellum whereby the CF input is thought to serve as an instructive 'teaching' signal that modifies PF synaptic input through induction of LTD (Marr, 1969).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by citation to Marr's work.

claim: The role of climbing fiber as a teaching signal remains a controversial component in the theory of cerebellar function and motor learning.
source: However, this remains a controversial component in the theory of cerebellar function and motor learning, and a corresponding description of dendritic coincidence detection from awake animals is still missing (Mauk et al., 1998; Najafi and Medina, 2013; Sakurai, 1987; Schonewille et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies discussing the controversy.

claim: A description of dendritic coincidence detection from awake animals is still missing.
source: However, this remains a controversial component in the theory of cerebellar function and motor learning, and a corresponding description of dendritic coincidence detection from awake animals is still missing (Mauk et al., 1998; Najafi and Medina, 2013; Sakurai, 1987; Schonewille et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Previous in vitro studies identified two dendritic mechanisms by which coincidence detection may occur, which depend on the strength and timing of coincident parallel fiber and climbing fiber stimulation.
source: Specifically, previous in vitro studies identified two dendritic mechanisms by which coincidence detection may occur, which depend on the strength and timing of coincident PF and CF stimulation (Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous in vitro work.

claim: The two dendritic coincidence detection mechanisms identified in vitro involved voltage-gated calcium channels and/or group one metabotropic glutamate receptors.
source: These mechanisms involved voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) and/or group one metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR1).
evidence: This describes specific molecular mechanisms identified in previous in vitro studies.

claim: How coincidence detection mechanisms occur during behavior remains to be determined.
source: How these processes occur during behavior remains to be determined.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: In vivo studies using calcium imaging found that climbing fiber-evoked calcium signals were enhanced during sensory stimulation in mice.
source: In vivo studies using calcium imaging found that CF-evoked calcium signals were enhanced during sensory stimulation (an air puff directed toward the eye) in mice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vivo studies.

claim: Graded non-climbing fiber sensory-evoked calcium signals were detected and proposed to be driven by parallel fiber input.
source: Notably, graded non-CF sensory-evoked calcium signals were detected and proposed to be driven by PF input (Najafi et al., 2014a; Najafi et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: More recent studies have failed to detect supralinear dendritic calcium signals triggered by coincident parallel fiber and climbing fiber input during sensory stimulation.
source: More recent studies, however, have failed to detect supralinear dendritic calcium signals triggered by coincident PF and CF input during sensory stimulation (Gaffield et al., 2019; Gaffield et al., 2018), challenging the role that PF input might play on the sensory-evoked dendritic calcium signals.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies that contradict earlier findings.

claim: Coincidence detection of parallel fiber and climbing fiber input remains to be confirmed in vivo.
source: Coincidence detection of PF and CF input remains to be confirmed in vivo.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge based on conflicting previous studies.

claim: It is unclear if the coincidence detection mechanisms previously described in vitro also occur in vivo and if so, how they occur and under what behavioral conditions.
source: Specifically, it is unclear if the coincidence detection mechanisms previously described in vitro also occur in vivo and if so, how they occur and under what behavioral conditions.
evidence: This identifies specific questions that the current study aims to address.

claim: A direct relationship between voltage and calcium signaling in spiny dendrites has not yet been explored in behaving animals due to technical limitations.
source: Furthermore, because of technical limitations, a direct relationship between voltage and calcium signaling in spiny dendrites has not yet been explored in behaving animals.
evidence: This identifies a technical limitation that has prevented previous studies from addressing this question.

claim: The study investigates the dendritic mechanisms that lead to the enhanced dendritic calcium signals in Purkinje neurons during sensory stimulation.
source: Specifically, we investigate the dendritic mechanisms that lead to the enhanced dendritic calcium signals in PNs during sensory stimulation.
evidence: This states the specific aim of the current study.

claim: A fast (2 kHz) two-photon imaging technique was developed to simultaneously record dendritic voltage and calcium signals from Purkinje neuron spiny dendrites in awake mice.
source: To study dendritic integration in vivo, we recently developed a fast (2 kHz) two-photon imaging technique to simultaneously record dendritic voltage and calcium signals from PN spiny dendrites in awake mice.
evidence: This describes the novel technical approach developed for the study.

claim: By recording dendritic voltage and calcium signals simultaneously, fast dendritic calcium spikes and slow depolarizing or hyperpolarizing synaptic inputs were recorded.
source: By recording dendritic voltage and calcium signals simultaneously we recorded fast dendritic calcium spikes and also slow depolarizing or hyperpolarizing synaptic inputs, which were confirmed using combined electrophysiology and pharmacological manipulation (Kuhn and Roome, 2019; Roome and Kuhn, 2018; Roome and Kuhn, 2019; Roome and Kuhn, 2020).
evidence: This describes the types of signals recorded and is supported by citations to previous work validating the approach.

claim: Single Purkinje neurons in lobule V of the cerebellar vermis were double labeled with voltage sensitive dye ANNINE-6plus and genetically encoded calcium indicator GCaMP6f.
source: Single PNs in lobule V of the cerebellar vermis were double labeled with voltage sensitive dye ANNINE-6plus and genetically encoded calcium indicator GCaMP6f, as described previously (Roome and Kuhn, 2018) (see Supplementary information).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for labeling neurons.

claim: A chronic cranial window with access port permitted two photon imaging, single neuron labeling, electrophysiology and drug delivery.
source: Briefly, a chronic cranial window with access port (Roome and Kuhn, 2014) permitted two photon imaging, single neuron labeling, electrophysiology and drug delivery (Figure 1a–e, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental preparation and is supported by reference to figures.

claim: Weak electrical stimulation (30 mA) evoked a depolarizing dendritic voltage signal corresponding to a sustained depolarization in membrane potential of approximately 3.8 ± 4.2 mV.
source: Weak electrical stimulation (30 mA) evoked a depolarizing dendritic voltage signal (average during stimulus; 1.8 ± 2.1% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, n = 26, 7 PNs), corresponding to a sustained depolarization in membrane potential of approximately 3.8 ± 4.2 mV, and a gradual increase in dendritic calcium (calcium peak; 18.3 ± 23.0% ΔF/F, time to peak; 92.3 ± 46.9 ms, mean ± SD, n = 26, 7 PNs), and relatively few DS events (3 ± 2 DS/100 ms, mean ± SD, n = 26, 7 PNs) (Figure 1i).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the electrical stimulation experiments.

claim: Strong electrical stimulation (300 mA) evoked a larger sustained depolarization corresponding to a depolarization in membrane potential of approximately 6.9 ± 4.2 mV.
source: Strong electrical stimulation (300 mA) evoked a larger sustained depolarization (average during stimulus, 3.3 ± 2.0% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, n = 26, 7 PNs, unpaired t-test, p=0.0148), corresponding to a depolarization in membrane potential of approximately 6.9 ± 4.2 mV, and a larger supralinear dendritic calcium signal with a delayed time to peak (calcium peak; 75.2 ± 55.0% ΔF/F, unpaired t-test, p=1.1 × 10−5, time to peak; 129.1 ± 26.1 ms, unpaired t-test, p=9.8 × 10−4, mean ± SD, n = 26, 7 PNs).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the electrical stimulation experiments with statistical testing.

claim: Strong electrical stimulation triggered dendritic spike events more consistently than weak stimulation.
source: Strong electrical stimulation also triggered DS events more consistently (5 ± 3 DS/100 ms, mean ± SD, n = 26, 7 PNs, Kolmogorov–Smirnov, p=0.0308) (see Figure 1j and k).
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing the effects of different stimulation strengths.

claim: A prolonged hyperpolarizing voltage signal followed the depolarization that increased with stimulus strength.
source: A prolonged hyperpolarizing voltage signal also followed the depolarization that increased with stimulus strength (average 100 ms following weak stimulus; −1.7 ± 2.7% ΔF/F, average 100 ms following strong stimulus; −4.7 ± 5.1% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, n = 26, 7 PNs, unpaired t-test, p=0.01), which we propose is due to feed forward inhibition that follow PF-evoked depolarization and/or intrinsic dendritic mechanisms, such as voltage- or calcium-activated potassium channels, as described in vitro (Martina et al., 2003; Mittmann et al., 2005; Otsu et al., 2014; Womack, 2004; Zagha et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a quantitative result with proposed mechanisms supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The depolarizing and hyperpolarizing voltage signals, dendritic complex spikes, dendritic spikes and calcium signals were all blocked following application of CNQX.
source: Accordingly, the depolarizing and hyperpolarizing voltage signals, DCSs, DSs and calcium signals were all blocked following application of CNQX (100 μM) confirming that these signals arise from EPSPs and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs) (see faint red and green traces in Figure 1j).
evidence: This is an experimental result from pharmacological manipulation confirming the synaptic origin of the signals.

claim: Dendritic calcium signals evoked by parallel fiber synaptic input have multiple calcium sources.
source: Taken together this indicates that dendritic calcium signals evoked by PF synaptic input have multiple calcium sources, as described previously in vitro (Denk et al., 1995; Eilers et al., 1995; Llano et al., 1991a; Sugimori and Llinás, 1990; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Multiple calcium sources likely include calcium influx gated by mGluR1 activation at parallel fiber-Purkinje neuron synapses.
source: These are likely to include calcium influx gated by mGluR1 activation at PF–PN synapses (Tempia et al., 2001), voltage-dependent DSs (Denk et al., 1995; Roome and Kuhn, 2018; Usowicz et al., 1992), and calcium released from internal stores (Llano et al., 1994; Llano et al., 1991a; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Dendritic spike events are generated by strong parallel fiber input.
source: Since PF and CF synaptic input constitute the only excitatory input to PN dendrites (Llano et al., 1991b), and DS events are blocked by CNQX (Figure 1j; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 7), have no corresponding somatic complex spike associated with CF input (Figure 1h), and are evoked by strong PF stimulation (Figure 1i–k), we conclude that the DS events are generated by strong PF input to the PN dendrites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence and anatomical knowledge.

claim: Parallel fiber input following a spontaneous climbing fiber event triggers additional dendritic spike events and results in a supralinear dendritic calcium signal.
source: As a proof of principle for dendritic coincidence detection of PF and CF input, Figure 1k shows an example of how PF input (here evoked by electrical stimulation) following a spontaneous CF event triggers additional DS events and results in a supralinear dendritic calcium signal.
evidence: This is demonstrated by an example shown in the figure.

claim: In total 54 Purkinje neurons in 23 mice were labeled.
source: In total 54 PNs in 23 mice were labeled and several PNs (up to 5) were labeled in the same mouse (Figure 2a).
evidence: This describes the sample size for the study.

claim: High intensity air puffs (pressure: 30 psi) were delivered via a glass capillary positioned 2 cm from the eye to evoke a reliable eye blink reflex in the ipsilateral eye.
source: High intensity air puffs (pressure: 30 psi) were delivered via a glass capillary positioned 2 cm from the eye to evoke a reliable eye blink reflex in the ipsilateral eye, which was monitored using a video camera (Figure 2b–d).
evidence: This describes the sensory stimulation protocol used in the study.

claim: Mice were naïve to the sensory stimulus receiving test stimuli (<5) before recording began and 5–30 stimuli during a single recording session.
source: Mice were naïve to the sensory stimulus receiving test stimuli (<5) before recording began and 5–30 stimuli (average of 13 recordings per PN) during a single recording session.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: During sessions, all air puffs were unexpected, triggering an eye blink reflex in the ipsilateral eye and no conditioned pre-stimulus eye blink responses were observed.
source: During sessions, all air puffs were unexpected, triggering an eye blink reflex in the ipsilateral eye and no conditioned pre-stimulus eye blink responses were observed, indicating that the mouse did not learn to expect the stimulus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral monitoring during experiments.

claim: Sensory stimulation evoked dendritic complex spikes, dendritic spikes and sustained depolarizing or hyperpolarizing signals.
source: Simultaneous voltage and calcium dendritic recordings revealed DCSs, DSs and sustained depolarizing or hyperpolarizing signals during sensory stimulation (Figure 2e–h and Figure 2—figure supplement 3), similar to those observed following electrical stimulation of PFs.
evidence: This is a primary observation from the sensory stimulation experiments.

claim: The dendritic signals observed were not evoked during voluntary eye blinks.
source: The dendritic signals we observed were not evoked during voluntary eye blinks or detected while the mouse was anesthetized (1% isoflurane) and presented with the same air puff stimuli, confirming their relationship to the sensory stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 5, respectively).
evidence: This is a control experiment confirming the specificity of the sensory-evoked signals.

claim: The dendritic signals observed were not detected while the mouse was anesthetized.
source: The dendritic signals we observed were not evoked during voluntary eye blinks or detected while the mouse was anesthetized (1% isoflurane) and presented with the same air puff stimuli, confirming their relationship to the sensory stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 5, respectively).
evidence: This is a control experiment confirming the specificity of the sensory-evoked signals.

claim: The amplitude and direction of evoked voltage signals were variable between individual Purkinje neurons and on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: The amplitude and direction (i.e., depolarizing or hyperpolarizing) of evoked voltage signals were variable between individual PNs and on a trial-by-trial basis (see Figure 2e–h and figure supplements for more examples).
evidence: This is an observation about the variability of the recorded signals.

claim: Combining all trials within the sampling region, the maximum change in dendritic voltage was positive (i.e., depolarizing) corresponding to an average deflection in membrane potential of approximately 6.1 ± 9.0 mV.
source: Note that combining all trials within our sampling region (Figure 1a), the maximum change in dendritic voltage was positive (i.e., depolarizing) (2.91 ± 4.3% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, 54 PNs, t-test, p=7.25 × 10−6) which corresponds to an average deflection in membrane potential of approximately 6.1 ± 9.0 mV.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the sensory stimulation experiments.

claim: Approximately 53% of voltage recordings displayed a depolarizing signal during the stimulus.
source: Approximately 53% of voltage recordings displayed a depolarizing signal during the stimulus (max Δ in dendritic voltage > + threshold); 14% showed hyperpolarizing voltage signals (max Δ in dendritic voltage < − threshold); 7% had a truncated signal that appeared to be a superposition of both depolarizing and hyperpolarizing signals (max Δ in dendritic voltage > + threshold, and < − threshold, at different time points during the stimulus); and 26% showed no response during the stimulus (did not reach threshold in either depolarizing or hyperpolarizing directions).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the distribution of response types.

claim: Depolarizing signals increased gradually throughout the stimulus, beginning 9 ± 3 ms after stimulus onset, and reaching a maximum after 101 ± 3 ms.
source: Depolarizing signals increased gradually throughout the stimulus, beginning 9 ± 3 ms (mean ± SD, n = 307) after stimulus onset, and reaching a maximum after 101 ± 3 ms, which is essentially at the stimulus offset.
evidence: This is a quantitative characterization of the temporal profile of depolarizing signals.

claim: Hyperpolarizing signals were sharper, and their onset occurred later, beginning 35 ± 2 ms after stimulus onset, and reaching a maximum hyperpolarization 57 ± 2 ms after stimulus onset.
source: Hyperpolarizing signals were sharper, and their onset occurred later, beginning 35 ± 2 ms (mean ± SD, n = 83) after stimulus onset, and reaching a maximum hyperpolarization 57 ± 2 ms (mean ± SD) after stimulus onset (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative characterization of the temporal profile of hyperpolarizing signals.

claim: The maximum change in dendritic voltage was similar between depolarizing, hyperpolarizing, and depolarizing + hyperpolarizing groups and significantly larger than the no response group.
source: The maximum change in dendritic voltage was similar between depolarizing (6.7 ± 4.7% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, n = 307), hyperpolarizing (6.1 ± 4.0 %ΔF/F, mean ± SD, n = 83), and depolarizing + hyperpolarizing groups (7.0 ± 4.2% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, n = 38) and significantly larger than the no response group (2.6 ± 1.0% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, n = 133), ANOVA, p<1.2 × 10−8, n = 561, 49 PNs (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between response groups with statistical testing.

claim: The time of eyelid closure was independent of response type.
source: The time of eyelid closure (measured from stimulus onset to maximum eyelid closure) was independent of response type (Figure 2—figure supplement 4); depolarized (128 ± 40 ms, mean ± SD), hyperpolarized (123 ± 44 ms, mean ± SD), depolarized + hyperpolarized (124 ± 32 ms, mean ± SD), and no response (139 ± 50 ms, mean ± SD) groups, Kruskal–Wallis ANOVA, p>0.35, n = 561, 49 PNs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing no correlation between dendritic response and behavioral response timing.

claim: A lack of dendritic voltage response was not due to a failure of the sensory stimulus, but rather that there was no detectable change in synaptic input to the Purkinje neuron dendrites.
source: This confirmed that a lack of dendritic voltage response was not due to a failure of the sensory stimulus, but rather that there was no detectable change in synaptic input to the PN dendrites.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results based on the independence of eyelid closure time and dendritic response.

claim: Individual Purkinje neurons displayed a trend toward a particular voltage response.
source: Individual PNs displayed a trend toward a particular voltage response (Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and see also Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is an observation about the consistency of responses within individual neurons.

claim: The majority of Purkinje neurons exhibited 'depolarizing' responses (36/54 PNs).
source: The majority of PNs exhibited 'depolarizing' responses (36/54 PNs), and the remaining PNs exhibited either 'hyperpolarizing' (6/54 PNs), both 'depolarizing + hyperpolarizing' (1/54 PNs), or 'no response' (11/54 PNs).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the distribution of response types across neurons.

claim: The average fraction of recordings across all Purkinje neurons showing their preferred response was 0.65 ± 0.18.
source: The average fraction of recordings across all PNs showing their preferred response was 0.65 ± 0.18 (mean ± SD, n = 54 PNs) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of response consistency within neurons.

claim: Evoked calcium signals from Purkinje neurons within the 'depolarizing' voltage response group were enhanced compared to spontaneous calcium signals.
source: Interestingly, we found this only to be true for PNs within the 'depolarizing' voltage response group (depolarizing spontaneous: 13 ± 10% ΔF/F; depolarizing evoked: 19 ± 14%ΔF/F, mean ± SD, ANOVA, p<6 × 10−8, 36 PNs) and the 'hyperpolarizing' voltage response group (hyperpolarizing spontaneous: 9 ± 7%ΔF/F; hyperpolarizing evoked: 18 ± 12%ΔF/F, mean ± SD, ANOVA, p<10−7, 6 PNs), but evoked calcium signals from PNs within the 'no response' group were not enhanced compared to spontaneous calcium signals (no response spontaneous: 11 ± 8%ΔF/F; no response evoked: 13 ± 9% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, ANOVA, p=0.99, 11 PNs) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of evoked and spontaneous calcium signals across different response groups.

claim: The voltage signals evoked by sensory stimulation were blocked following application of CNQX (100 μM).
source: The voltage signals evoked by sensory stimulation were blocked following application of CNQX (100 μM) (Figure 2k and Figure 2—figure supplement 7) and also Na+ channel blocker Lidocaine (0.2%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 8), confirming that these dendritic signals were driven by synaptic input (and not movement artifacts).
evidence: This is an experimental result from pharmacological manipulation confirming the synaptic origin of the signals.

claim: The voltage signals evoked by sensory stimulation were blocked following application of Na+ channel blocker Lidocaine (0.2%).
source: The voltage signals evoked by sensory stimulation were blocked following application of CNQX (100 μM) (Figure 2k and Figure 2—figure supplement 7) and also Na+ channel blocker Lidocaine (0.2%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 8), confirming that these dendritic signals were driven by synaptic input (and not movement artifacts).
evidence: This is an experimental result from pharmacological manipulation confirming the synaptic origin of the signals.

claim: The maximum change in dendritic voltage measured within a 200 ms window after stimulus onset was significantly reduced under CNQX conditions.
source: The maximum change in dendritic voltage (measured within a 200 ms window after stimulus onset) was significantly reduced under CNQX conditions; control (8.0 ± 7.3% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, n = 45), CNQX (4.4 ± 3.4% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, n = 46), unpaired t-test, p=0.003, n = 91, 5 PNs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the pharmacological manipulation experiment.

claim: The eyelid closure time following CNQX application was not significantly different to control conditions.
source: The eyelid closure time following CNQX application was not significantly different to control conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 7); control (134 ± 40 ms, mean ± SD, n = 45); CNQX (156 ± 44 ms, mean ± SD, n = 37), Kolmogorov–Smirnov, p=0.12, n = 82, 5 PNs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing that CNQX did not affect the behavioral response.

claim: Application of CNQX and Lidocaine blocked dendritic complex spikes and dendritic spikes.
source: Application of CNQX and Lidocaine also blocked DCSs and DSs (Figure 2—figure supplements 7 and 8).
evidence: This is an experimental result from pharmacological manipulation.

claim: Sensory stimulation evokes graded depolarizing and hyperpolarizing voltage signals in Purkinje neuron spiny dendrites.
source: From the observations made thus far we conclude that sensory stimulation evokes graded depolarizing and hyperpolarizing voltage signals in PN spiny dendrites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results presented.

claim: On average, sensory-evoked dendritic voltage signals have a relatively small amplitude (6.1 ± 9.0 mV), below threshold for triggering voltage-gated calcium channels.
source: On average these dendritic voltage signals have a relatively small amplitude (6.1 ± 9.0 mV), below threshold for triggering VGCCs, have a much slower time course compared to DCSs and DSs and are blocked by CNQX (Figure 2k and Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a characterization of the sensory-evoked voltage signals based on the experimental data.

claim: Sensory-evoked dendritic voltage signals originate primarily from parallel fiber synaptic input.
source: Since CF synaptic input reliably evokes rapid DCSs (Roome and Kuhn, 2018) and noting their similarity to the voltage signals evoked by PF stimulation shown in Figure 1i–k, we conclude that these signals originate primarily from PF synaptic input.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison with climbing fiber-evoked signals and parallel fiber stimulation results.

claim: On average the sensory stimulus-evoked parallel fiber input gives rise to a depolarizing signal across the Purkinje neuron dendrites (global depolarization) that begins 9 ± 3 ms after stimulus onset.
source: On average the sensory stimulus-evoked PF input gives rise to a depolarizing signal across the PN dendrites (global depolarization) that begins 9 ± 3 ms after stimulus onset, which is consistent with rapid and dense GC responses to sensory stimulation (Giovannucci et al., 2017; Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and supported by citations to previous work on granule cell responses.

claim: The sensory stimulation-evoked hyperpolarizing dendritic signals are in agreement with an increase in molecular layer interneuron activity, and feed forward inhibition evoked by sensory stimulation.
source: The sensory stimulation-evoked hyperpolarizing dendritic signals are also in agreement with an increase in MLI activity, and feed forward inhibition evoked by sensory stimulation (Chu et al., 2012; Gaffield et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hyperpolarizing signals supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The trial-by-trial variability in Purkinje neuron dendritic voltage responses is likely to result from an interplay between parallel fiber and molecular layer interneuron synaptic inputs driven by the mossy fiber pathway.
source: The trial-by-trial variability in PN dendritic voltage responses that we detect is likely to result from an interplay between these two synaptic inputs driven by the MF pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed variability based on known cerebellar circuitry.

claim: Sustained voltage signals (depolarizing and hyperpolarizing) during sensory stimulation were detected with no coincident dendritic complex spikes or dendritic spikes in several recording trials.
source: In several recording trials we detected sustained voltage signals (depolarizing and hyperpolarizing) during sensory stimulation with no coincident DCSs or DSs (see Figure 3a for example).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Dendritic calcium signals in Purkinje neurons are predominantly mediated by P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels triggered during dendritic complex spikes or dendritic spikes.
source: While dendritic calcium signals in PNs are predominantly mediated by P/Q-type VGCCs triggered during DCSs or DSs (Usowicz et al., 1992), additional mechanisms also contribute to dendritic calcium signaling at PF–PN synapses, which do not require DCS or DS events.
evidence: This is established knowledge about calcium signaling in Purkinje neurons supported by citation.

claim: Glutamate released during parallel fiber input can activate mGluR1s and trigger calcium influx.
source: For example, glutamate released during PF input can activate mGluR1s and trigger calcium influx (Tempia et al., 2001) and modulate low threshold T-type VGCCs (Ait Ouares and Canepari, 2020; Hildebrand et al., 2009; Otsu et al., 2014), and also trigger calcium release from intracellular stores (Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about calcium signaling mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: Glutamate released during parallel fiber input can modulate low threshold T-type voltage-gated calcium channels.
source: For example, glutamate released during PF input can activate mGluR1s and trigger calcium influx (Tempia et al., 2001) and modulate low threshold T-type VGCCs (Ait Ouares and Canepari, 2020; Hildebrand et al., 2009; Otsu et al., 2014), and also trigger calcium release from intracellular stores (Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about calcium signaling mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: Glutamate released during parallel fiber input can trigger calcium release from intracellular stores.
source: For example, glutamate released during PF input can activate mGluR1s and trigger calcium influx (Tempia et al., 2001) and modulate low threshold T-type VGCCs (Ait Ouares and Canepari, 2020; Hildebrand et al., 2009; Otsu et al., 2014), and also trigger calcium release from intracellular stores (Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about calcium signaling mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: Whether spike-independent calcium signals are involved in dendritic signaling in Purkinje neurons during sensory stimulation has not been confirmed.
source: Whether or not these signals are involved in dendritic signaling in PNs during sensory stimulation has not been confirmed.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Averaging recordings with no dendritic complex spikes or dendritic spikes revealed a small but clear increase in dendritic calcium during sensory stimulation that reached a maximum 135.8 ± 48.3 ms after stimulus onset.
source: Averaging these recordings revealed a small but clear increase in dendritic calcium during the sensory stimulation that reached a maximum 135.8 ± 48.3 ms after stimulus onset (dendritic calcium at stimulus offset relative to baseline: 1.8 ± 2.8% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, n = 59, t-test, p=5.9 × 10−6) (Figure 3b), which was blocked following application of CNQX (100 μM) (Figure 3c); average calcium at stimulation offset under CNQX conditions was −0.2 ± 2.3% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, and not significantly different from baseline, t-test, p=0.59, n = 36, 5 PNs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing spike-independent calcium signals during sensory stimulation.

claim: The spike-independent calcium signal during sensory stimulation was blocked following application of CNQX (100 μM).
source: Averaging these recordings revealed a small but clear increase in dendritic calcium during the sensory stimulation that reached a maximum 135.8 ± 48.3 ms after stimulus onset (dendritic calcium at stimulus offset relative to baseline: 1.8 ± 2.8% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, n = 59, t-test, p=5.9 × 10−6) (Figure 3b), which was blocked following application of CNQX (100 μM) (Figure 3c); average calcium at stimulation offset under CNQX conditions was −0.2 ± 2.3% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, and not significantly different from baseline, t-test, p=0.59, n = 36, 5 PNs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from pharmacological manipulation confirming the synaptic origin of the calcium signal.

claim: There is a voltage–calcium relationship during sensory stimulation in the absence of dendritic spikes (Pearson's r = 0.71, p=4.51 × 10−10).
source: Calculating the average voltage and calcium signal over the full sensory stimulus, on a trial-by-trial basis, revealed the voltage–calcium relationship (n = 59, Pearson's r = 0.71, p=4.51 × 10−10) (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing a correlation between voltage and calcium signals.

claim: Parallel fiber-evoked dendritic voltage signals generate voltage-dependent dendritic calcium signals in the absence of climbing fiber input.
source: This confirms that PF-evoked dendritic voltage signals (described in Figure 2) generate voltage-dependent dendritic calcium signals in the absence of CF input.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the voltage-calcium relationship observed in the absence of dendritic spikes.

claim: Sensory stimulation is known to trigger enhanced calcium signals in Purkinje neuron dendrites of the cerebellar vermis, compared to spontaneous calcium signals.
source: Sensory stimulation is known to trigger enhanced calcium signals in PN dendrites of the cerebellar vermis, compared to spontaneous calcium signals (Najafi et al., 2014a; Najafi et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: The voltage signals that trigger enhanced calcium signals during sensory stimulation have not been directly explored in awake animals.
source: While various mechanisms have been shown to modulate dendritic calcium signals in PNs, including MLI activity (Callaway et al., 1995; Gaffield et al., 2018; Kitamura and Häusser, 2011), PF activity (Wang et al., 2000), and graded CF input (Gaffield et al., 2019; Roh et al., 2020), the voltage signals that trigger these calcium signals have not been directly explored in awake animals.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: An increase in frequency of both dendritic complex spikes and dendritic spikes was detected during the sensory stimulus.
source: Importantly, we detected an increase in frequency of both DCSs and DSs during the sensory stimulus (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a primary observation from the sensory stimulation experiments.

claim: Average dendritic complex spike and dendritic spike frequencies during the stimulus was 5.73 ± 5.51 Hz and 1.24 ± 0.77 Hz respectively.
source: Average DCS and DS frequencies during the stimulus was 5.73 ± 5.51 Hz and 1.24 ± 0.77 Hz (mean ± SD), respectively; a relative increase in DCS and DS frequency of 5.5 and 9.5 times, respectively (see Figure 4b inset).
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing the increase in spike frequency during sensory stimulation.

claim: The average timing of dendritic complex spike and dendritic spike signals after stimulus onset was 43.3 ± 22.1 ms and 53.3 ± 24.5 ms respectively.
source: The average timing of DCS and DS signals after stimulus onset was 43.3 ± 22.1 ms (mean ± SD, n = 414) and 53.3 ± 24.5 ms (mean ± SD, n = 92) respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative characterization of the timing of spike events during sensory stimulation.

claim: There was a distinct increase in the probability of detecting dendritic complex spikes and dendritic spikes during the stimulus compared to the pre-stimulus time window.
source: There was a distinct increase in the probability of detecting DCSs and DSs during the stimulus compared to the pre-stimulus time window; DCS only (pre-stimulus: 11.5 ± 1.2%, stimulus: 49.3 ± 1.7%); DS only (pre-stimulus: 0.8 ± 0.4%, stimulus: 7.6 ± 1.1%); paired DCS + DS signals (pre-stimulus: 0.3 ± 0.2%, stimulus: 5.9 ± 0.9%) (mean ± SD, n = 688, Kolmogorov–Smirnov, p=7.3 × 10−79).
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing the increased probability of spike events during sensory stimulation.

claim: On average, evoked calcium signals were enhanced relative to non-evoked calcium signals (relative calcium peak; 1.4 ± 0.6, 51 PNs, 365 recordings, t-test, p=1.5 × 10−5).
source: In agreement with previous studies (Gaffield et al., 2019; Najafi et al., 2014a; Najafi et al., 2014b), we found that on average, evoked calcium signals (i.e., signals triggered during the stimulus) were enhanced relative to non-evoked calcium signals (i.e. signals occurring before the stimulus) (relative calcium peak; 1.4 ± 0.6, 51 PNs, 365 recordings, t-test, p=1.5 × 10−5) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result confirming previous findings with the current dataset.

claim: Calcium peaks were on average larger following evoked dendritic complex spike signals compared to the non-evoked dendritic complex spike signals.
source: Calcium peaks were on average larger following evoked DCS signals compared to the non-evoked DCS signals (non-evoked: 12.6 ± 9.3% ΔF/F, n = 1624, evoked: 20.8 ± 15.1% ΔF/F, n = 333, mean ± SD, unpaired t-test, p=1.6 × 10−37) (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison showing enhanced calcium signals during sensory stimulation.

claim: There was an increase in the total number of dendritic spikelets following each evoked dendritic complex spike signal compared to non-evoked dendritic complex spike signals.
source: Accordingly, the corresponding dendritic voltage recordings showed an increase in the total number of dendritic spikelets following each evoked DCS signal compared to non-evoked DCS signals, evident through a positive shift in the spikelet count probability distribution (Kolmogorov–Smirnov, p=1.85 × 10−5) (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing increased spiking activity during sensory stimulation.

claim: When only single dendritic complex spike signals were permitted, the peak calcium of evoked signals remained enhanced compared to non-evoked signals.
source: Interestingly, when only single DCS signals were permitted, the peak calcium of evoked signals remained enhanced compared to non-evoked signals (non-evoked: 11.9 ± 8.1%ΔF/F, n = 1292, evoked: 19.7 ± 14.2%ΔF/F, n = 203, mean ± SD, unpaired t-test, p=3.8 × 10−28) (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing that the enhancement is not solely due to multiple climbing fiber inputs.

claim: The time to peak for evoked calcium signals was delayed compared to non-evoked calcium signals.
source: The time to peak for evoked calcium signals was also delayed compared to non-evoked calcium signals (non-evoked: 37.7 ± 26.3 ms, n = 1292, evoked: 69.0 ± 44.9 ms, n = 203, mean ± SD, unpaired t-test, p=2.7 × 10−42) (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1, for a comparison of all dendritic calcium signals described so far).
evidence: This is a quantitative result characterizing the temporal dynamics of evoked calcium signals.

claim: The differences in the calcium signal time-course are indicative of an additional source of calcium following the evoked dendritic complex spike, causing a delayed and enhanced calcium peak.
source: These differences in the calcium signal time-course are indicative of an additional source of calcium following the evoked DCS, causing a delayed and enhanced calcium peak, while the similarity in spikelet numbers between evoked and non-evoked DCS suggests this additional calcium source is spike-independent.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The enhanced calcium signal is not due to an increase in climbing fiber input frequency, or an increase in dendritic spiking, caused by stronger climbing fiber input.
source: Thus, the enhanced calcium signal is not due to an increase in CF input frequency, or an increase in dendritic spiking, caused by stronger CF input, but through an additional mechanism that does not require DCSs or DSs, such as described in Figure 3, or potentially calcium released from internal stores (Llano et al., 1994; Llano et al., 1991a; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and supported by citations to potential mechanisms.

claim: There is a clear asymmetric and supralinear relationship between the timing of dendritic complex spike and dendritic spike signals and their corresponding calcium signals.
source: Analysis revealed a clear asymmetric and supralinear relationship between the timing of DCS and DS signals and their corresponding calcium signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of paired spike events.

claim: The relative calcium peak was maximum when dendritic spike followed dendritic complex spike events and was independent of the number of dendritic complex spike spikelets.
source: The relative calcium peak was maximum when DS followed DCS events and was independent of the number of DCS spikelets (two spikelets: 1.8 ± 1.3 [n = 13]; three spikelets: 2.0 ± 1.2 [n = 15]; four spikelets: 1.7 ± 0.9 [n = 6]; five spikelets: 1.3 ± 0.3 [n = 3], mean ± SD, measured in the 80 ms time window following the DCS, ANOVA, p>0.7763).
evidence: This is a quantitative result characterizing the supralinear calcium signal from paired spike events.

claim: The average relative calcium peak (2.0 ± 0.1) is maximum when dendritic spike follow dendritic complex spike signals by 28.3 ± 5.4 ms.
source: By fitting a two-term Gaussian function (Figure 4i) we estimate that the average relative calcium peak (2.0 ± 0.1) is maximum when DS follow DCS signals by 28.3 ± 5.4 ms (mean ± SD).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fitting the timing relationship of paired spike events.

claim: An additional dendritic spike evoked by parallel fiber input following a dendritic complex spike evoked by climbing fiber input can enhance the dendritic calcium signal supralinearly (potentially by more than 100% relative to the dendritic complex spike event alone) depending on the timing of the two events.
source: This means that an additional DS (evoked by PF input) following a DCS (evoked by CF input) can enhance the dendritic calcium signal supralinearly (potentially by more than 100% relative to the DCS event alone) depending on the timing of the two events.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the quantitative analysis of paired spike events.

claim: Paired dendritic complex spike + dendritic spike signals evoked by coincident climbing fiber and parallel fiber input act to enhance the dendritic calcium signal supralinearly, and this enhancement is dependent on the timing of paired events.
source: Thus, we conclude that paired DCS + DS signals evoked by coincident CF and PF input act to enhance the dendritic calcium signal supralinearly, and this enhancement is dependent on the timing of paired DCS + DS events.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental results.

claim: Paired dendritic complex spike + dendritic spike signals are relatively rare (detected in only 5.9 ± 0.9% of recordings).
source: However, paired DCS + DS signals are relatively rare (detected in only 5.9 ± 0.9% of recordings), suggesting an additional coincidence detection mechanism at work.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation suggesting the existence of additional mechanisms.

claim: A prominent depolarization beginning before the evoked dendritic complex spike event was revealed by averaging voltage traces within each evoked spikelet group; this 'pre-DCS' signal was not detected before non-evoked dendritic complex spike signals.
source: Averaging voltage traces within each evoked spikelet group revealed a prominent depolarization beginning before the evoked DCS event; this 'pre-DCS' signal was not detected before non-evoked DCS signals however (see black arrowheads in Figure 5c).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of voltage traces aligned to spike events.

claim: The evoked pre-dendritic complex spike depolarization amplitude was independent to the number of dendritic complex spike spikelets.
source: The evoked pre-DCS depolarization amplitude was independent to the number of DCS spikelets (two spikelets: 1.31 ± 1.84% ΔF/F; three spikelets: 1.35 ± 1.93% ΔF/F; four spikelets: 1.47 ± 2.22% ΔF/F; five spikelets: 1.29 ± 1.14% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, ANOVA, p>0.52) (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing that the pre-spike depolarization is consistent across different spike amplitudes.

claim: Using the voltage-calcium relationship and the average pre-dendritic complex spike voltage, an average increase in calcium baseline of 0.8 ± 1.5% ΔF/F would be predicted.
source: Using the voltage-calcium relationship determined in Figure 3, and the average pre-DCS voltage across all spikelet groups; 1.36 ± 1.89% ΔF/F (approximately 2.9 ± 4.0 mV, mean ± SD), we would predict an average increase in calcium baseline of 0.8 ± 1.5% ΔF/F.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the voltage-calcium relationship established earlier.

claim: The average calcium peak is much larger during evoked dendritic complex spike signals compared to non-evoked dendritic complex spike signals comprising the same number of spikelets.
source: The average calcium peak, however, is much larger during evoked DCS signals compared to non-evoked DCS signals comprising the same number of spikelets.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of calcium signals aligned to spike events.

claim: The difference between evoked and non-evoked calcium peaks increased supralinearly with the number of dendritic complex spike spikelets.
source: Furthermore, the difference between evoked and non-evoked calcium peaks increased supralinearly with the number of DCS spikelets (non-evoked vs. evoked, two spikelets: 6.2 ± 3.2% ΔF/F vs. 10.1 ± 5.5% ΔF/F; three spikelets: 11.1 ± 5.7% ΔF/F vs. 17.0 ± 7.7% ΔF/F; four spikelets: 16.4 ± 8.6% ΔF/F vs. 25.1 ± 11.7% ΔF/F; five spikelets: 18.5 ± 10.2% ΔF/F vs. 39.3 ± 17.1% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, ANOVA, p<0.002) (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing a supralinear relationship between spike number and calcium enhancement.

claim: The linear sum of non-evoked dendritic complex spike calcium peak and predicted increase in calcium baseline could not account for the supralinear enhancement in calcium peak during evoked dendritic complex spike signals.
source: In this case, the linear sum of non-evoked DCS calcium peak and our predicted increase in calcium baseline ('+ cal.') could not account for the supralinear enhancement in calcium peak during evoked DCS signals (non-evoked + cal. vs. evoked, ANOVA, p<0.043) (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing that the enhancement cannot be explained by simple linear summation.

claim: Activation of mGluR1s by coincident parallel fiber and climbing fiber input is known to drive supralinear calcium signals at parallel fiber-Purkinje neuron synapses in cerebellar slices.
source: Activation of mGluR1s by coincident PF and CF input is known to drive supralinear calcium signals at PF–PN synapses in cerebellar slices (Wang et al., 2000), but their contribution to PN dendritic signaling has not been explored in vivo.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous in vitro studies supported by citation.

claim: The contribution of mGluR1 to Purkinje neuron dendritic signaling has not been explored in vivo.
source: Activation of mGluR1s by coincident PF and CF input is known to drive supralinear calcium signals at PF–PN synapses in cerebellar slices (Wang et al., 2000), but their contribution to PN dendritic signaling has not been explored in vivo.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: After application of AIDA, sensory-evoked calcium signals were significantly reduced.
source: After application of AIDA, sensory-evoked calcium signals were significantly reduced (control: 24.4 ± 12.3% ΔF/F, AIDA: 17.9 ± 9.3% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, unpaired t-test, p=0.025) (Figure 5h).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the pharmacological manipulation experiment.

claim: Non-evoked calcium signals were not significantly altered by AIDA application.
source: Non-evoked calcium signals, however, were not significantly altered (control: 10.6 ± 6.5% ΔF/F, AIDA: 9.5 ± 5.5% ΔF/F, mean ± SD, unpaired t-test, p=0.116), indicating that the contribution of mGluR1 activity to the calcium signal is specific to sensory-evoked calcium signals when CF and PF inputs coincide, and we propose that mGluR1s are activated at PF–PN synapses, where the PF and CF synaptic potentials converge.
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing the specificity of mGluR1 contribution to evoked signals.

claim: The mGluR1 antagonist did not directly affect climbing fiber and parallel fiber input.
source: As in Figure 4c, there was a clear increase in signal probability during the stimulus compared to pre-stimulus time windows under both control and AIDA conditions, but we detected no difference between control vs. AIDA conditions (for either pre-stimulus or stimulus groups), indicating that the mGluR1 antagonist did not directly affect CF and PF input (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the pharmacological manipulation experiment showing no effect on synaptic input.

claim: There was no significant effect of AIDA on evoked dendritic voltage signaling.
source: There was also no significant effect of AIDA on evoked dendritic voltage signaling, supporting the conclusion that these signals are predominantly AMPA mediated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the pharmacological manipulation experiment.

claim: The probability distribution for the total number of spikelets following evoked dendritic complex spike was shifted toward lower numbers under AIDA conditions.
source: However, we found that the probability distribution for the total number of spikelets following evoked DCS was shifted toward lower numbers under AIDA conditions.
evidence: This is a result from the pharmacological manipulation experiment.

claim: Unlike control conditions, the probability distributions for the total number of spikelets following evoked and non-evoked dendritic complex spike signals were no longer significantly different following AIDA application.
source: Consequently, unlike control conditions (Figure 5i), the probability distributions for the total number of spikelets following evoked and non-evoked DCS signals were no longer significantly different following AIDA application (Figure 5j).
evidence: This is a result from the pharmacological manipulation experiment showing the effect of mGluR1 blockade.

claim: mGluR1 activity enhances spikelet generation during evoked dendritic complex spike signals.
source: This suggests that mGluR1 activity enhances spikelet generation during evoked DCS signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the effect of AIDA on spikelet probability distributions.

claim: Three interplaying dendritic coincidence detection mechanisms modulate calcium signals at the Purkinje neuron dendritic level.
source: To summarize, we identify three interplaying dendritic coincidence detection mechanisms that modulate calcium signals at the PN dendritic level.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: Purkinje neuron dendrites integrate excitatory postsynaptic potentials from parallel fiber input, which can result in a graded (voltage-dependent) calcium signal.
source: PN dendrites integrate EPSPs from PF input (Figure 2), which can result in a graded (voltage-dependent) calcium signal (Figure 3; cf. Figure 1).
evidence: This is a summary of one of the coincidence detection mechanisms identified in the study.

claim: The voltage-dependent dendritic calcium signal is continually regulated by excitatory postsynaptic potential and inhibitory postsynaptic potential.
source: We expect that the voltage-dependent dendritic calcium signal is continually regulated by EPSP and IPSP and the first mechanism of dendritic coincidence detection occurs when this voltage-dependent calcium signal coincides with a CF-evoked calcium signal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of how the first coincidence detection mechanism operates.

claim: The second coincidence detection mechanism is through parallel fiber-evoked dendritic spike events, whose frequency increases during the sensory stimulus, and when paired with dendritic complex spike act to enhance the climbing fiber-evoked calcium signal in a time-dependent manner.
source: The second mechanism is through the PF-evoked DS events, whose frequency increases during the sensory stimulus, and when paired with DCS act to enhance the CF-evoked calcium signal in a time-dependent manner (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary of the second coincidence detection mechanism identified in the study.

claim: The greatest enhancement in calcium signal occurred when the dendritic spike followed the dendritic complex spike by ~28 ms.
source: We found the greatest enhancement in calcium signal occurred when the DS followed the DCS by ~28 ms, which appears to be in contrast to in vitro experiments, where the maximal enhancement in calcium signal was detected when PF stimulation preceded CF stimulation (Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a quantitative result characterizing the timing dependence of the second coincidence detection mechanism.

claim: The timing of the dendritic spike event does not indicate the onset of parallel fiber input, but the moment that the threshold in membrane potential is reached to trigger the dendritic spike event.
source: However, we note that the DS events are due to a culmination of integrated PF input, and so the timing of the DS event does not indicate the onset of PF input, but the moment that the threshold in membrane potential is reached to trigger the DS event, and so it is expected that PF input onset begins sooner.
evidence: This is an interpretation explaining the apparent discrepancy with in vitro results.

claim: On average parallel fiber input onset precedes climbing fiber input during sensory stimulation by ~34 ms.
source: Indeed, we found that on average PF input onset precedes CF input during sensory stimulation by ~34 ms, as shown in Figures 2j and Figure 4b, and as indicated by the pre-DCS depolarization in Figure 5c.
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing the temporal relationship between parallel fiber and climbing fiber inputs.

claim: Parallel fiber-evoked dendritic spike signals play a unique role in modulating dendritic calcium signals during sensory stimulation.
source: While PF-evoked DS signals are relatively rare in awake mice (Roome and Kuhn, 2018), we found that their frequency increased 9.5 times during sensory stimulation, and their impact on the dendritic calcium signal was supralinear. Thus, we propose PF-evoked DS signals play a unique role in modulating dendritic calcium signals during sensory stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed increase in dendritic spike frequency and their supralinear effect on calcium signals.

claim: The additional parallel fiber-evoked dendritic spike could be viewed as a correction to the climbing fiber-evoked dendritic complex spike signal, supplementing an otherwise 'too weak' dendritic complex spike signal with extra dendritic spikes.
source: In fact, the additional PF-evoked DS could be viewed as a correction to the CF-evoked DCS signal, supplementing an otherwise 'too weak' DCS signal with extra DSs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional role of parallel fiber-evoked dendritic spikes.

claim: The third coincidence detection mechanism is through mGluR1 activity.
source: The third mechanism we describe is through mGluR1 activity (Figure 5), which is known to trigger supralinear calcium signals when PF and CF inputs are conjunctively activated, and thereby modify PF–PN synaptic strength (Sarkisov and Wang, 2008; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a summary of the third coincidence detection mechanism identified in the study.

claim: mGluR1 activity can directly influence dendritic complex spike generation by the climbing fiber input and the time-course of the resulting dendritic calcium signal, specifically during evoked dendritic complex spike events.
source: It was interesting to find that mGluR1 activity can directly influence DCS generation by the CF input and the time-course of the resulting dendritic calcium signal, specifically during evoked DCS events (c.f. Figure 5h and j).
evidence: This is a novel finding about the role of mGluR1 in modulating climbing fiber-evoked signals.

claim: An interaction between mGluR1 activity and climbing fiber-evoked spikelet generation has previously been postulated.
source: Such an interaction between mGluR1 activity and CF-evoked spikelet generation has previously been postulated (Batchelor and Garthwaite, 1997; Tempia et al., 2001) and is likely mediated through their interaction with T and P/Q-type VGCCs (Hildebrand et al., 2009; Otsu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work that postulated this interaction.

claim: The climbing fiber input has historically been viewed as an 'all-or-none' type event.
source: The CF input has historically been viewed as an 'all-or-none' type event (Eccles et al., 1966), such that CF-evoked EPSPs are identical from one CF input to the next (provided the PN membrane potential is held constant).
evidence: This is a historical perspective on climbing fiber function supported by citation.

claim: The 'signal-to-noise' problem asserts that if Purkinje neuron dendritic responses to climbing fiber were identical, 'evoked' and 'spontaneous' climbing fiber inputs would be indistinguishable at the level of the Purkinje neuron dendrite.
source: This problem, referred to as the 'signal-to-noise' problem (Llinás et al., 1997), asserts that if PN dendritic responses to CF were identical, 'evoked' and 'spontaneous' CF inputs would be indistinguishable at the level of the PN dendrite.
evidence: This describes a theoretical problem in cerebellar function supported by citation.

claim: Given that climbing fiber inputs are delivered continuously at a rate of ~1 Hz, the information encoded by 'teaching' signals should be lost among the noise of spontaneous climbing fiber input.
source: Given that CF inputs are delivered continuously at a rate of ~1 Hz, the information encoded by 'teaching' signals should be lost among the noise of spontaneous CF input (see Najafi and Medina, 2013 and Zang and De Schutter, 2019 for review).
evidence: This describes the consequence of the signal-to-noise problem supported by citations to reviews.

claim: A growing body of evidence has proved that climbing fibers are not such inefficient teachers, showing that climbing fiber-evoked dendritic calcium signals are in fact graded, and that 'evoked' calcium signals are enhanced compared to 'spontaneous' signals.
source: A growing body of evidence, however, has proved that CFs are not such inefficient teachers, showing that CF-evoked dendritic calcium signals are in fact graded, and that 'evoked' calcium signals are enhanced compared to 'spontaneous' signals.
evidence: This summarizes recent evidence that challenges the historical view of climbing fiber function.

claim: A recent study has proposed that calcium signals in Purkinje neuron dendrites evoked by sensory stimulation are graded entirely by the strength of climbing fiber input, essentially from outside of the cerebellum, without direct contribution from the mossy fiber pathway.
source: In contrast to our findings, a recent study has proposed that calcium signals in PN dendrites evoked by sensory stimulation are graded entirely by the strength of CF input, essentially from outside of the cerebellum, without direct contribution from the MF pathway (Gaffield et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes an alternative hypothesis from a recent study supported by citation.

claim: The strength of climbing fiber input has a powerful influence on spikelet generation in Purkinje neuron dendrites and consequently on dendritic calcium signals.
source: We agree that the strength of CF input has a powerful influence on spikelet generation in PN dendrites (Davie et al., 2008) and consequently on dendritic calcium signals (Gaffield et al., 2019; Roh et al., 2020; Roome and Kuhn, 2018), and it cannot be excluded that differences in recording location and/or sensory stimulation may favor differing mechanisms for modulating calcium signals in PN dendrites.
evidence: This acknowledges the role of climbing fiber strength supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There is a clear nonlinear relationship between climbing fiber-evoked dendritic complex spikes and the resulting dendritic calcium signal, specific to climbing fiber input evoked by sensory stimulation.
source: However, as seen in Figure 5, we find a clear nonlinear relationship between CF-evoked DCSs and the resulting dendritic calcium signal. Importantly, this nonlinear voltage–calcium relationship was specific to CF input evoked by sensory stimulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study showing a nonlinear relationship specific to evoked signals.

claim: Coincident parallel fiber and climbing fiber input evokes supralinear dendritic calcium signals via mechanisms within the Purkinje neuron dendrite; through voltage-gated calcium channels (parallel fiber-evoked dendritic spike events), and activation of mGluR1s.
source: Here we show how coincident PF and CF input evokes supralinear dendritic calcium signals via mechanisms within the PN dendrite; through VGCCs (PF-evoked DS events), and activation of mGluR1s.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study summarizing the mechanisms of coincidence detection.

claim: Independent of the climbing fiber input, coincidence detection mechanisms can modulate the downstream dendritic calcium signal and significantly enhance the information that can be transmitted by the evoked climbing fiber event.
source: Independent of the CF input, these coincidence detection mechanisms can modulate the downstream dendritic calcium signal and we propose this significantly enhances the information that can be transmitted by the evoked CF event.
evidence: This is a proposed functional implication of the coincidence detection mechanisms.

claim: If evoked calcium signals in Purkinje neuron dendrites are graded entirely by the strength of climbing fiber input, their dynamic range would suffer from a similar 'signal-to-noise' problem.
source: In the case where evoked calcium signals in PN dendrites are graded entirely by the strength of CF input, we would expect that their dynamic range would suffer from a similar 'signal-to-noise' problem, such that there remains a limited range in the information that can be transmitted or 'taught' to a single PN.
evidence: This is a logical argument about the limitations of climbing fiber-only modulation.

claim: Evoked dendritic calcium signals can be adjusted at the Purkinje neuron dendritic level, within the cerebellar circuitry, in a way that accounts for instructive signals carried by mossy fibers via parallel fiber input.
source: An important functional implication of the coincidence detection mechanisms described here is that evoked dendritic calcium signals can be adjusted at the PN dendritic level, within the cerebellar circuitry, in a way that accounts for instructive signals carried by MFs via PF input.
evidence: This is a proposed functional implication of the study's findings.

claim: In principle dendritic calcium signals can be fine-tuned with higher temporal and spatial precision, potentially at the level of single spines and branchlets throughout the entire dendritic tree.
source: In principle dendritic calcium signals can be fine-tuned with higher temporal and spatial precision, potentially at the level of single spines and branchlets throughout the entire dendritic tree (Denk et al., 1995), in far more detail than could be attained through enhanced CF input alone, as predicted by computational approaches (Zang and De Schutter, 2019; Zang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a proposed functional implication supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Spontaneous climbing fiber events show a large degree of spatiotemporal variability across dendritic segments in awake mice.
source: Indeed, spontaneous CF events show a large degree of spatiotemporal variability across dendritic segments in awake mice (Roome and Kuhn, 2018) and we predict the spatiotemporal patterns of evoked DCS, modulated by PF input, to be particularly important in conveying information encoded by coincident PF and CF input events, during sensory stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and includes a prediction about the importance of spatiotemporal patterns.

claim: The combination of the various dendritic mechanisms may function to control the size and spread of the dendritic response to the coincidence detection event, thereby defining the 'dendritic computational unit' and potentially, the extent of synaptic plasticity at parallel fiber-Purkinje neuron synapses.
source: The combination of the various dendritic mechanisms we describe here may function to control the size and spread of the dendritic response to the coincidence detection event (the dendritic calcium signal in this case), thereby defining the 'dendritic computational unit' (Zang et al., 2018) and potentially, the extent of synaptic plasticity at PF–PN synapses.
evidence: This is a proposed functional implication supported by citation to computational work.

claim: The coincidence detection processes and supralinear dendritic calcium signals are triggered by sensory stimulation yet occur seemingly continuously; during sensory stimulation in awake naïve mice, and not only during motor learning of a specific task.
source: It is intriguing that the coincidence detection processes and supralinear dendritic calcium signals we describe here are triggered by sensory stimulation yet occur seemingly continuously; during sensory stimulation in awake naïve mice, and not only during motor learning of a specific task, such as eye blink conditioning.
evidence: This is an observation about the conditions under which the coincidence detection mechanisms operate.

claim: In vitro studies have shown how membrane potential and timing of coincident parallel fiber and climbing fiber synaptic inputs are critical for modulating calcium signaling and synaptic plasticity at parallel fiber-Purkinje neuron synapses.
source: In vitro studies have shown how membrane potential and timing of coincident PF and CF synaptic inputs are critical for modulating calcium signaling and synaptic plasticity at PF–PN synapses (Ly et al., 2016; Piochon et al., 2012; Sarkisov and Wang, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous in vitro studies supported by citations.

claim: Purkinje neuron dendrites and their spines are highly sensitive to calcium levels, which can in turn determine the direction of synaptic plasticity at parallel fiber-Purkinje neuron synapses.
source: PN dendrites and their spines are highly sensitive to calcium levels, which can in turn determine the direction of synaptic plasticity at PF–PN synapses (Coesmans et al., 2004; Jörntell and Hansel, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about calcium-dependent plasticity supported by citations.

claim: To constantly fine-tune plasticity at parallel fiber-Purkinje neuron synapses, calcium signals are continuously graded at the global and subcellular dendritic level.
source: We expect that to constantly fine-tune plasticity at PF–PN synapses, calcium signals are continuously graded at the global and subcellular dendritic level.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for ongoing plasticity based on the study's findings.

claim: The coincident activity of climbing fiber and parallel fiber synaptic input combined with intrinsic dendritic mechanisms allow for a full dynamic spatiotemporal range in dendritic calcium signaling.
source: The coincident activity of CF and PF synaptic input (and PF driven feed forward inhibition via MLIs [Gaffield et al., 2018; Kitamura and Häusser, 2011]) combined with intrinsic dendritic mechanisms (VGCCs and mGluR1s) allow for a full dynamic spatiotemporal range in dendritic calcium signaling, which we propose serve as efficient mechanisms for decoding the information transmitted by CF-evoked 'teaching' signals.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study about the functional implications of the coincidence detection mechanisms.

claim: The combined activity of coincidence detection mechanisms becomes more apparent during heightened sensory input, as indicated by their enhanced cooperation during sensory-evoked eye blink responses.
source: Here, we establish that the combined activity of these mechanisms becomes more apparent during heightened sensory input, as indicated by their enhanced cooperation during sensory-evoked eye blink responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion about when the coincidence detection mechanisms are most active.
